div.head: IV Atr 2.10
div.ab: Et non licebat eis aliquod forceapum facere burhmannis et dare toll' suum et in sancto natali Domini duos grisengos pannos et unum brunum et decem libras piperis et cirotecas quinque hominum et duos caballinos tonellos aceto plenos; et totidem in pascha.

Et non licebat eis aliquod forceapum facere burhmannis, et dare toll' suum et in sancto natali Domini duos grisengos pannos et unum brunum et decem libras piperis et cirotecas quinque hominum et duos caballinos tonellos aceto plenos; et totidem in pascha.

Doch durften sie nicht den [Londoner] Bürgern [zum Schaden] irgend welchen Vorkauf üben und [mussten] ihren Zoll geben und zu Weihnachten zwei graue Tücher und ein braunes und 10 Pfund Pfeffer und fünf Männerhandschuhe und zwei für Pferde tragbare Fässchen voll Essig; und ebenso viel zu Ostern.

But they were not allowed to engage in any forestalling [to the detriment] of the [London] citizens, and [had to] give their toll, and at Christmas two grey cloths and one brown, and 10 pounds of pepper and five men's gloves and two small casks of vinegar such as a horse can carry; and as much again at Easter.

But they were not allowed any right of pre-emption over the burgesses, and [they had] to pay their toll, and at Christmas two lengths of grey cloth and one length of brown and 10 pounds of pepper and five pairs of gloves and two saddle-kegs of vinegar, and the same at Easter.
div.note: Clause number corrected from ‘2.1’ to ‘2.10’ (stored as a number, which dropped the final zero).

Vgl. Gl London 37; Handel 16a. Steenstrup hält auch das Wort forceap aus Nord. forköp entlehnt; Danelag 379. [Die Bed. ist nicht ‘widerrechtliche Abgabe’ oder ‘Erpressung’ (Ducange, Schmid, Riley)]. Mittelengl. und Anglofrz. ist forechepe, forscheper belegt. Foranus non faciat forchep civi; Londoner Marktrecht 12. Jhs. bei Cunningham Growth of industry 542 = Bateson in EHR 1902, 718; ähnlich Hans. Urkb. III n. 600

Cf. Gl London 37; Handel 16a. Steenstrup holds that the word forceap too is borrowed from Norse forköp; Danelag 379. [The meaning is not ‘unlawful levy’ or ‘extortion’ (Ducange, Schmid, Riley)]. In Middle English and Anglo-French forechepe, forscheper are attested. Foranus non faciat forchep civi; London market law of the 12th cent. in Cunningham Growth of industry 542 = Bateson in EHR 1902, 718; similarly Hans. Urkb. III n. 600

grisengus kennt Ducange aus England auch sonst für ‘grau’; ‘gray cloth’ ist Englisch (wie ‘grau Leinen’) für ‘ungebleicht und ungefärbt Tuch’; vgl. Dänisch griseum pannum ad unam tunicam ‘Hemdentuch’ bei Steenstrup Danelag 378. Die Grautucher in Basel und Ulm sind Wollhändler; die Zunft der Marner faciunt pannos de lana griseos; in Hansi. Geschichtsbl. 1902, 99. [Da pannus nicht ‘Pelz’ sein kann, und da zum folgenden brunum ‘Tuch’ zu ergänzen nötig ist, fällt die andere Deutung ‘Grauwerk’ (pellicium grisonis a. 1276 bei Round King's serjeants 258) fort; vgl. Gl Tuch 3; o. 2, 3²]

grisengus is known to Ducange from England elsewhere too, meaning ‘grey’; ‘gray cloth’ is English (like ‘grau Leinen’) for ‘unbleached and undyed cloth’; cf. Danish griseum pannum ad unam tunicam ‘shirt-cloth’ in Steenstrup Danelag 378. The Grautucher in Basel and Ulm are wool-dealers; the guild of the Marner faciunt pannos de lana griseos; in Hansi. Geschichtsbl. 1902, 99. [Since pannus cannot be ‘fur’, and since ‘cloth’ must be supplied with the following brunum, the other interpretation, ‘grey fur’ (pellicium grisonis a. 1276 in Round King's serjeants 258), falls away; cf. Gl Tuch 3; above 2, 3²]

Vgl. Gl Pfeffer. Aus Deutschland und Flandern belegt diese Abgaben als Symbol der Anerkennung herrschaftlicher Marktgewalt ausführlich Höhlbaum III 381⁷; vgl. II S. 123, auch Schulte Gesch. malt. Handels I 73.—Der Englische Ältermann der Deutschen Hanseaten in London erhielt von diesen ein jährliches Geschenk in einem Paar Handschuh; Engel in Hans. Geschi. Bl. 1914, 198

Cf. Gl Pfeffer. These dues, as a symbol of the recognition of a lord's authority over the market, are documented in detail from Germany and Flanders by Höhlbaum III 381⁷; cf. II p. 123, also Schulte Gesch. malt. Handels I 73.—The English alderman of the German Hanseatics in London received from them an annual gift of a pair of gloves; Engel in Hans. Geschi. Bl. 1914, 198
caballinus ist spätes Latein. Mengl. kommt horsecharche, horselode ‘Pferdeladung’ vor; Mätzner
caballinus is late Latin. In Middle English horsecharche, horselode ‘horse-load’ occurs; Mätzner
Cf. Norse forkjøb, Steenstrup, Danelag, p. 378 f., and see Bateson, E.H.R., 1902, p. 718.
The construction is difficult to understand. Liebermann suggests that the original (A.S.) may have been elliptical.

Liebermann points out that, since they pay toll at Christmas and Easter, German merchants must have wintered in England. According to the twelfth-century rules for foreign merchants no Lorrainer might dwell in the city more than 40 days, unless a storm of wind or some evil delayed him, or he stayed for a debt which was withheld from him, see § 6 (E.H.R. 1902, p. 500), and cf. Lib. Lond. 9, 1 (Liebermann, i. p. 675). Norwegians and Danes, however, had right of sojourn for a year (E.H.R. p. 502).

grisengus pannus is understood as ‘minever’ by Schmid, following Du Cange, s.v. griseum, and translated ‘grey skin’ by Ballard (Domesday Boroughs, p. 116); pannus however, as Liebermann points out, means ‘cloth’ not ‘skin.’
Cf. Lib. Lond. 8, 1.
i.e. kegs portable on horseback; caballinus is a late Latin word.
